content: Postpartum haemorrhage is a leading cause of maternal mortality worldwide. To prevent this condition, the routine use of uterotonic agents during the third stage of labour has been widely recommended. A proposed method involves administering these uterotonic agents through the umbilical vein after the baby is delivered. While the therapeutic use of this approach has been studied, its routine or prophylactic use has not been thoroughly evaluated. The objective of this study was to compare the effects of umbilical vein injection of a saline solution, either alone or combined with a uterotonic drug, against alternative solutions (with or without uterotonic agents), expectant management, or other methods for the routine management of the third stage of labour. The aim was to assess the impact on maternal and perinatal outcomes using the best available evidence. To gather relevant data, a search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register up to January 31, 2012, along with a review of reference lists from retrieved studies. Randomised controlled trials comparing umbilical vein injection of saline (with or without uterotonic drugs) to other methods were included in the analysis. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility and quality of the trials, and data extraction was performed by two reviewers, with accuracy checks conducted subsequently. A total of nine studies involving 1118 women were included in the review. Four different comparisons were identified. The primary comparison involved six studies with 394 women, which evaluated the effects of umbilical vein injection of normal saline combined with oxytocin versus normal saline alone. The other three comparisons each included only one study. In the primary comparison, no significant differences were observed in any of the reported outcomes, including the number of women requiring blood transfusion, the incidence of manual removal of the placenta, the amount of blood loss, or the duration of the third stage of labour. Subgroup analyses based on the total volume of solution administered and the dose of oxytocin also showed no evidence of any differences. The other three comparisons, each based on a single study, did not provide sufficient relevant information. The authors concluded that the routine use of oxytocin or other uterotonic agents with normal saline via umbilical vein injection is not recommended based on the current evidence. Further research is needed to evaluate the effectiveness of this method in the routine management of the third stage of labour.
